summary: A survey of the state of graphics on the ARPANET for newcomers. It reviews past work, notes how little had been written on the subject, and adds the author's own thoughts about using the network's many computers for graphics.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reviews early ARPANET graphics work and proposes a model for connecting programs to different displays. The model separates application work, network messages and device-specific display handling.

subtitle: A survey of network graphics proposals and a model for coordinating displays and programs.

tldr.problem: Earlier graphics proposals covered separate details, while the network's varied computers and displays called for a general system model.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys prior work and proposes a model connecting an application, input and output routines, display drivers, a display and graphic data bases.
tldr.outcome: The proposed model favors supporting many configurations over minimizing response time and leaves substantial detailed work open.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 285 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The document presents a model for discussion rather than a complete protocol specification.

sections.title: Why a General Model Is Needed
sections.content:
The author notes that few entries in the NIC collection concerned graphics and presents the paper as an overview for newcomers. The network offers many processors, so the machine running the main application need not also handle the display.

A general graphics language can describe output, while a device-specific processor translates it for a particular terminal. Interactive input adds another challenge because the application and display may hold different versions of a picture.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can use different computers for the application and the display. A general model can describe how they exchange pictures and user input.

sections.title: Earlier Graphics Work
sections.content:
Early proposals used a small set of drawing commands, but later discussion called for a richer language that could represent logical and pictorial structure, subpictures and display modes. The RFC reviews work on network graphics, attention handling, tablet input, the Graphics Loader and NETCRT.

For interactive graphics, an attention message should identify the device, the data being supplied and the data itself. Local processing can update a display quickly, but the main process must learn about changes when it needs to keep its own picture data current.
sections.plainLanguage: Early graphics proposals grew from simple drawing commands into a more general language. Interactive systems also need a way to report input and local changes back to the application.

sections.title: The Proposed Graphics Model
sections.content:
The model has a PROCESS, the graphics application, with INPUT and OUTPUT routines. At the display end, INPUT and OUTPUT drivers translate between network-standard messages and the display's device-specific data. Drawing information flows toward the display, and attention information flows back to the process.

The process and display drivers may each keep a Graphic Data Base. The RFC describes PROGRAM graphics, where the main process constructs the picture, and LOCAL graphics, where the display updates its own data and informs the process.
sections.plainLanguage: The application sends drawing information through routines and drivers to the display. Input travels back, and local changes can be reported so the application can keep its data in step.

sections.title: Generality and Message Structure
sections.content:
The author prioritizes a wide mix of configurations rather than minimum response time. Drivers should split processing between themselves and the main process according to the display being used. Non-interactive graphics can skip attention processing.

Graphics messages should have a distinguishing header, a byte identifying the body type, a count of body bytes and the body. The RFC presents a framework for evaluating proposals and says detailed work remains.
sections.plainLanguage: The model aims to work with many device arrangements rather than to guarantee the fastest response. It describes how messages can identify their content and length.
